Daniel Burnham was an American architect and urban planner who lived from 1846 to 1912. His visionary leadership transformed Chicago into a modern metropolis and established principles of grand-scale urban design that influenced American cities for generations. He is best known for masterminding the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and championing monumental Beaux-Arts classicism and the "City Beautiful" movement, which used grand public spaces, classical architecture, and comprehensive planning to elevate civic life.

Rising from modest origins, Burnham became Chicago's preeminent architect during the city's explosive growth. His partnership with John Wellman Root, until Root's death in 1891, established his reputation for ambitious large-scale projects. He served as chief architect and director of works for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, orchestrating a "White City" of neoclassical buildings and grand plazas that captivated millions of visitors and defined the Beaux-Arts aesthetic for America. He designed the Flatiron Building in New York in 1902, an innovative triangular structure that became an iconic symbol of urban modernity and demonstrated his mastery of the steel-frame skyscraper.

Burnham pioneered comprehensive urban planning, developing master plans for Chicago, San Francisco, and Washington D.C. that emphasized grand avenues, public parks, monumental civic centers, and integrated transportation. He promoted the "City Beautiful" movement, which held that aesthetically elevated public spaces and classical architecture could improve civic morality, reduce social conflict, and create ordered, harmonious cities—a philosophy reflecting Gilded Age optimism and anxiety about urban chaos. He trained numerous architects in his firm who became influential in their own right, spreading his principles across American cities. His maxim "Make no little plans; they have no magic to stir men's blood" became a rallying cry for ambitious urban development, influencing twentieth-century city planning, though his classical ideals eventually gave way to modernism.
